#library(tidyverse)

## Example 2: Platypus in Australia

Where can you find the strange platypus in Australia?

![[Image Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Platypus-sketch.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Platypus-sketch.jpg){width="60%"}

## Platypus in Australia

```{r not to run this code, eval=FALSE}
# Data extracted from ALA with this code
# Note that package ALA4Ris being replaced by package galah
# install.packages("galah")
library(galah)
ala_config(atlas = "Australia", download_reason_id=)
l <- ala_species("Platypus")

taxa <- select_taxa("Ornithorhynchus anatinus", counts = TRUE)

platypus <- ala_occurrences(taxa = taxa)

platypus <- platypus %>% rename(
  longitude = decimalLongitude,
  latitude = decimalLatitude
)
save(platypus, file="data/platypus.rda")
```

```{r load the platypus obervation data, echo=TRUE}
load(here::here("data/platypus.rda"))
platydata <- platypus
ggplot(data=platydata) + geom_point(aes(x=longitude, y=latitude))
```

## Platypus in Australia

```{r Add some transparency to see density of locations, echo=TRUE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, out.width = "80%"}
ggplot(data=platydata) + geom_point(aes(x=longitude, y=latitude), alpha=0.1)
```

We can make the data look a bit more realistic with `coord_map`.

::: notes
If you are good at recognising the shape of Australia, you might realise that the sightings are all along the east coast and Tasmania. There is a strange location, that looks like someone saw one in Antarctica! We might need to filter this observation out later, because its extremely unlikely to have been found that far south.
:::

## Platypus in Australia

::: columns
::: {.column width="25%"}
```{r making a map projection, echo=F, fig.width = 3, fig.height = 6, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(data=platydata) + 
  geom_point(aes(x=longitude, y=latitude), alpha=0.1) +
  coord_map()
```
:::
::: {.column width="75%"}
```{r making a map projection, echo=T, eval = F,fig.show=F, fig.height=10, out.width="100%"}
```

- Adding a map layer would help!
- Install the `leaflet` R package to create interactive maps
:::
:::

## Leaflet Platypus Maps

```{r leaflet map, echo=TRUE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
library(leaflet)
platydata %>%
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude), !(eventDate=="")) %>%
  leaflet() %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius=1, opacity = 0.5, color = "orange", label = ~eventDate,
    lat = ~latitude, lng = ~longitude) 
```

## Temporal trend

Plot sightings over time (`eventDate`). The first step is to convert `eventDate` into a date time object.

```{r create a date variable, echo=TRUE}
library(lubridate)
platydata <- platydata %>% 
  mutate(eventDate = ymd_hms(eventDate))
```

## Temporal trend
::: notes
then we can simply plot occurrence over time.
:::

```{r show sightings over time, echo=TRUE, fig.height = 1, fig.width = 8, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(data=platydata) +
  geom_point(aes(x=eventDate, y=1))
```

There are some records dating back before 1800. There were only records from 1770! And these first records are in the database!


##  Temporal trend

There are a LOT more sightings in more recent years than in the 18th and 19th century, but this database has an amazing history!

```{r show jittered sightings over time, echo=TRUE, fig.height = 2, fig.width = 8, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(data=platydata) +
  geom_jitter(aes(x=eventDate, y=1), alpha = .2)
```


## Temporal trend

Let's focus on records since 1900, and count the sightings/year.

::: columns
::: column
```{r focus on records since 1900 and count the number for each year, echo=F, out.width="100%"}
platydata1900 <- platydata %>% 
  filter(year>1900) %>%
  count(year) 
ggplot(data=platydata1900) +
  geom_point(aes(x=year, y=n))
```
:::
::: column
```{r focus on records since 1900 and count the number for each year, echo=TRUE, eval=F}
```
:::
:::

```{r solution code for filtering on location and time, eval=FALSE}
# Check odd cases
platydata %>% filter(latitude < (-50)) 
# These just have the lat/long wrong
platydata %>% filter(eventDate < ymd("1850-01-01")) 
```

## Temporal trend

Add a trend line.


::: columns
::: column
```{r add a trend line,echo=F, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(data=platydata1900, 
       aes(x=year, y=n)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=F)
```
:::
::: column
```{r add a trend line, echo=TRUE, eval=F}
```
:::
:::

## Your turn {.inverse .middle}

`r countdown::countdown(10)`

Make sure you can make all the plots shown in this session, and then tackle the next set of tasks: 

- Change the dotplot into a density plot, to focus on the locations of frequent sightings.
- Do you learn anything different than from the scatterplot?

```{r solution code to density plot on map, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
ggmap(oz) + 
  geom_density2d(data=platydata, aes(x=longitude, y=latitude), 
              colour="orange") 
```

::: notes
Not a lot different. It shows perhaps high density regions around Melbourne, Brisbane and south of Sydney. These match high population sites, though, and maybe reiterates the sampling being convenience sampling. We miss the smaller areas of sightings, like northern Queensland.
:::


## Your turn {.inverse .middle}

Platypus are mostly found on the east coast of the country, but there is a population close to Adelaide in south Australia. Why is this? (You might need to do some sleuthing with a web search engine to answer this.)

## Your turn {.inverse .middle}

*Discussion question:* Was there a population explosion in 1980 and 2004? Is the population of platypus increasing since 1900, and decreasing in the last decade?

- Subset the data to 1950-2020
- Create a new variable for decade
- Make a map separately for each decade - the `facet_wrap` function can help here.

```{r solution code for exploring population trend, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
platydata_50_10 <- platydata %>% filter(year>1949, year<2020) %>%
  mutate(decade = cut(year, breaks=seq(1950, 2020, 10),
   include.lowest=TRUE, 
   labels=c("50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80-89", "90-99", "00-09", "10-19")))
ggmap(oz) + geom_point(data=platydata_50_10, mapping=aes(x=longitude, y=latitude), colour="orange", alpha=0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~decade)
```
